solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ranting crowd in turn succeeded breaking into club

indicators.note: turned round, the word runs backwards

parts.note: a mob is a crowd; turned round it gives BOM
a bat is a club, as in cricket or baseball
s. = succeeded, the abbreviation in family trees

explanation.surface: An angry mob barges into a club, shouting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ranting' is read as a noun here: bombast is ranting, puffed-up talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombast is pompous, inflated talk, which is what ranting amounts to.

clue.text: I throw up over match official, one Simon

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' sends the letters from bottom to top
in a down clue, one piece sits over (above) the next

parts.note: VAR = video assistant referee in football

explanation.surface: A sick fan throws up over the referee at a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw up' pretends to mean vomit; split it, and I + LOB go up the grid. Simon Bolivar liberated much of South America.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Bolivar is the famous Simon of that surname, so 'one Simon' points to him.

clue.text: Wildly enthusiastic about new libertine one found in bed

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it

parts.note: mad about something = wildly keen on it
a rake is a dissolute man

explanation.surface: Someone is besotted with a new rake they found in their bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a flower bed, not a bedroom one: the mandrake is a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandrake is a plant, so one might be found growing in a garden bed.

clue.text: Time to eat a very succulent growth

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: It is time to tuck into something very juicy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succulent' looks like praise for a meal; it is the botanical sense, a fleshy desert plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The agave is a spiky succulent plant, the source of tequila.

clue.text: Put fine glue on my doodah

indicators.note: each piece is put on the one before, building the word in order

parts.note: a fine thread is a thin one

explanation.surface: An instruction to glue a thin layer onto some gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: Doodah and thingummy are both words for something whose name you have forgotten.
explanation.definitionFit: A doodah is a whatsit, a thingummy: a stand-in name for an unnamed object.

clue.text: Spender rarely missed beer, half of each

indicators.note: only half of each of the two words is kept

explanation.surface: A man who seldom bought a round rarely went without his beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful description: a miser is someone who spends only rarely.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser is a person who spends as little and as rarely as possible.

clue.text: Lose track of road kill

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI in crosswords

explanation.surface: Losing track of an animal hit by a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Road kill' reads as one dead animal; split it into two words. The M1 is Britain's main motorway, so crosswords often clue MI as 'road'.
explanation.definitionFit: To mislay something is to put it down and lose track of where it is.

clue.text: Aimless wandering, concerned with earthquake

indicators.note: the letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: Someone drifting about in worry after a quake.
explanation.walkthrough: Seismal is a rarer form of seismic.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismal means relating to earthquakes, like seismic.

clue.text: Pipe up, rebel?

definitions.meaning: a vertical pipe carrying water or gas upward, named for the direction it runs
one who rises up in revolt

explanation.surface: Should a rebel speak out?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipe up' looks like the verb 'speak up'; it is a pipe that runs up.
explanation.definitionFit: A riser is an upward pipe, and one who rises against authority is a riser too.

clue.text: Los Angeles Gazette finally covers bridge game

indicators.note: take the last letter of Gazette

parts.note: to bridge a gap is to cross it

explanation.surface: A newspaper in Los Angeles runs a column on the card game bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge game' pretends to be the card game; bridge is the verb CROSS, and the definition is just 'game'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team game played with netted sticks.

clue.text: Edges away, keeling over exhausted

indicators.note: the outside letters of the word are removed

parts.note: keeling over = FALLING, whose edges are F and G

explanation.surface: Someone collapses and sidles away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edges away' reads as moving off sideways; it is an instruction to strip the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British idiom: after a hard day you are all in, with nothing left to give.

clue.text: Displaced area in girl's haunches and in the waist

indicators.note: the A is moved to a new place in MAID'S

parts.note: girl's = MAID'S; its A (area) is displaced to the front, making AMIDS

explanation.surface: Something about a girl's hips and waistline.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'waist' is a ship's: the middle section of the deck. Only the A moves; the rest of MAID'S stays put.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidships means in the middle of a ship, the part sailors call the waist.

clue.text: First person to go in to admire brown study

parts.note: to revere is to admire deeply

explanation.surface: A visitor is first in line to admire a study in a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: A brown study is a state of deep, absent-minded thought, not a room.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a daydream, the same lost-in-thought state as a brown study.

clue.text: School music award missing year, a choir's last

indicators.note: the award is missing the year, so its Y is left out
take the last letter of choir

parts.note: GRAMMY, the US music award, without Y (year)

explanation.surface: A school choir misses out on a music prize this year.
explanation.walkthrough: A grammar school is a selective secondary school in Britain, so 'School' alone can mean GRAMMAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar is short for grammar school, a kind of British school.

clue.text: Sitting astride modest conveyance hard, a few make strong impression

parts.note: a trike is a humble three-wheeler

explanation.surface: A few people riding a humble vehicle hard make a big impact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sitting astride' is read with its subject, 'a few', coming last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike home is to hit the mark, making a strong impression.

clue.text: Nothing is gained by hanging about and sucking up

parts.note: to hover is to hang about

explanation.surface: A cynic says loitering and fawning get you nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucking up' sounds like flattery; it is vacuum cleaning (Hoover is a vacuum brand).
explanation.definitionFit: Hoovering is vacuuming, which literally sucks up dirt.

clue.text: No end of obstruction for co-operating parties

indicators.note: the last letter is removed

parts.note: an obstruction is a BLOCK, which loses its end letter K

explanation.surface: Endless blocking tactics in a coalition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' usually means 'a great deal of'; here it means lose the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of parties or nations acting together.

clue.text: Dispatch salad plant, having wrapped it

indicators.note: something wrapped is enclosed

explanation.surface: Send off the salad greens once they are wrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatch' looks like a verb, send; it is the noun meaning speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Celerity is swiftness, as is dispatch in 'acted with dispatch'.

clue.text: With order of merit covering uniform, eat soup

parts.note: OM = Order of Merit, a British honour
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet; OM takes its place

explanation.surface: A decorated officer in uniform eats soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is part of the instruction: take CONSUME and put OM where the U was.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by kind: consommé is one particular soup, a clear meat broth.

clue.text: English vineyard's white, a bit off

parts.note: a cru is a vineyard, from French wine terms; 's = is, joining

explanation.surface: An English white wine that has gone slightly bad.
explanation.walkthrough: The wine talk hides a colour: 'a bit off' means off-white, not spoiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru, the colour of unbleached linen, is a shade just short of true white, hence 'a bit off'.

clue.text: Stream smooth computer image

parts.note: an icon is a small image on a screen

explanation.surface: Streaming a slick picture on a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stream' looks like a verb about video; it is the small river Caesar crossed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rubicon is a stream in northern Italy, famous from Caesar's crossing.

clue.text: Powerful expression being cut back, aim only for resolution

indicators.note: the word is written backwards
AIM ONLY is resolved into a new order

parts.note: to lop is to cut; written back, POL

explanation.surface: A forceful speech is edited down to a single purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Powerful' is mathematical: a polynomial is an expression built from powers of a variable.
explanation.definitionFit: A polynomial is an algebraic expression made of terms raised to powers.

clue.text: In a perfect world, I mooch around rear of house

indicators.note: take the last letter of house
mooching around something means circling it

parts.note: to mooch is to dawdle, dally

explanation.surface: Someone's dream is to potter about the back of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: To mooch, in British English, is to wander about idly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'ideally, we'd leave early' says what would happen if things went perfectly.

clue.text: Little pet I don't know catches a church mouse

parts.note: a pup is a young dog
er is the noise of hesitation

explanation.surface: A puppy, somehow, has caught a mouse in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor as a church mouse' is the idiom, so a church mouse is someone penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: A pauper is a very poor person, as poor as a church mouse.

clue.text: I'm thinking black fury brings offence

parts.note: um is the noise of someone thinking

explanation.surface: A dark temper, the speaker muses, causes offence.
explanation.walkthrough: To take umbrage is to take offence.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mostly heard in the idiom 'take umbrage', meaning take offence.

clue.text: Overturn cage in middle of studio

indicators.note: take the middle letters of studio

explanation.surface: Someone knocks over a cage in a studio.
explanation.walkthrough: STUDIO has six letters, so its middle is the pair UD.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend is to turn upside down, overturn.

clue.text: Regret rounding on crowd manipulator

indicators.note: to round is to turn round

parts.note: a mass of people is a crowd
to rue is to regret; turned round, EUR

explanation.surface: A demagogue who rabble-rouses comes to regret it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crowd manipulator' reads as a demagogue; the definition is 'manipulator' alone, one who manipulates muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseur manipulates the body's muscles.

clue.text: Crew, you shouldn't have giant fish

parts.note: to man a ship is to crew it
ta is British slang for thanks, as said on receiving a gift

explanation.surface: A crew is presented with a huge fish as a present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have!' is what you say on getting a gift: thanks, or TA in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the manta ray, with a wingspan up to seven metres, is one of the biggest fish in the sea.

clue.text: Anomaly of one working behind bar

parts.note: bar = except, as in 'all bar one'

explanation.surface: An odd sight: someone working behind a pub bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub counter; it is the preposition meaning except.
explanation.definitionFit: An exception is an anomaly, something that doesn't fit the rule.

clue.text: Cold temperature on Scottish island, mostly fine

indicators.note: most of the word, last letter dropped

parts.note: MULL, an island of the Inner Hebrides, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A weather report: cold on a Scottish island but mostly fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' is weather talk in the surface; the definition is the penalty, as a verb or noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To mulct is to fine someone, or extract money from them.

clue.text: One giving name getting through entrance

explanation.surface: A guest gives their name to get through the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a doorman checking a guest list.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: donors give money, blood or organs, so 'one giving' fits.

clue.text: Seriously hoarse, missing a line

explanation.surface: Someone is badly hoarse and forgets a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seriously hoarse' reads as one phrase; 'Seriously' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: grave means serious, so 'gravely ill' is seriously ill.
